name: THE EDAM AND WEEP BURGER (served with edam cheese and raw onion)

recipe.history:
Edam cheese traces its origins to the small harbor town of Edam in the province of North Holland in the Netherlands, where it has been produced since at least the fourteenth century. Named for the town itself, Edam was one of the most widely traded cheeses in the world during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, prized by sailors and merchants alike for its low fat content, firm texture, and extraordinary resistance to spoilage — qualities that made it ideal for long ocean voyages. Traditionally formed into spheres and coated in a red paraffin wax for export (though the domestic version is left uncoated), Edam is made from partially skimmed cow's milk, giving it a mild, slightly nutty, and faintly salty flavor that deepens beautifully with age. The Dutch were so proud of their cheese trade that Edam became a symbol of Dutch commercial ingenuity and culinary identity, appearing in still-life paintings alongside tulips and herring as a marker of national prosperity.

As Dutch settlers and traders brought their foodways to the New World in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, Edam made the transatlantic crossing alongside them, finding its way into American pantries and taverns. While Edam never achieved the supermarket ubiquity of American or cheddar in the United States, it carved out a steady presence in delicatessens, specialty grocers, and the kitchens of those who appreciated a meltable, mild cheese with genuine character. The burger world discovered Edam relatively quietly — not with the fanfare that surrounded blue cheese or pepper jack — but bartenders and short-order cooks found that its gentle creaminess when melted provided a refined counterpoint to beef's iron-rich boldness. Paired with raw onion, whose sulfurous sharpness cuts cleanly through fat, the combination became a quiet classic of the discerning burger builder's repertoire.

I remember the first time I really understood raw onion on a burger. I was maybe eleven years old, standing at the counter of a roadside diner somewhere on the New Jersey Turnpike, and the cook — a big man with forearms like ham hocks — slapped a thin-sliced white onion ring onto a just-assembled burger without asking, tucking it under the lid of the bun like it was the most natural thing in the world. I almost protested — onions were the enemy at that age — but something stopped me, and I took that first bite. The crunch, the eye-watering sharpness, the way it cut right through the richness of the beef and the slick of yellow mustard: it was a revelation. Years later, when I started experimenting with Edam on burgers, I kept coming back to that memory. The cheese needed something alive and biting to wake it up, and raw onion does exactly that — it is the sharpest possible contrast to Edam's quiet, creamy mildness, and together they make something unexpectedly electric.

Cooking a burger to medium rare — an internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is not a preference or a suggestion; it is the only philosophically defensible position available to a person who respects both the animal and themselves. At medium rare, the fat within the patty has begun to render and self-baste the meat from the inside, the myoglobin retains its rosy, iron-forward depth, and the texture remains yielding and almost voluptuous rather than compressed and dry. To cook a burger beyond this point is to destroy, deliberately and needlessly, everything that makes ground beef worth eating. The Edam and Weep Burger demands this standard above all others: the cheese must melt into a still-soft patty, pooling in the crevices of the meat rather than sitting atop a grey puck. Medium rare is not recklessness — it is respect.
ingredients: 480g bread flour, plus more for dusting
1 large egg, beaten with 1 tbsp water, for egg wash
225g Edam cheese, rind removed, sliced thin
1 large white onion, sliced paper-thin into rounds
softened unsalted butter, for toasting buns
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook. Add warmed milk, water, and the whole egg; mix on low until shaggy, about 2 minutes.

2. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time with the mixer running on medium. Increase to medium-high and knead until the dough is smooth, elastic, and pulls away from the bowl sides cleanly, about 8 minutes.
3. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise at room temperature until doubled, 1 to 1.5 hours.

4. Punch down dough and divide into 6 equal portions (approximately 140g each). Shape each into a tight ball by pulling the surface taut and pinching at the bottom. Place on parchment-lined baking sheets, spacing 3 inches apart. Cover loosely and let proof until puffy and nearly doubled, about 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush proofed buns with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake until deep golden brown, 18 to 20 minutes. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely.
6. Make the sauce: Whisk together mayonnaise, Dijon, white wine vinegar, sugar, and salt in a small bowl until smooth. Refrigerate until needed.

7. Prepare the raw onion: Place sliced onion rounds in a bowl of ice water and let soak for 20 minutes. This removes some of the harsh sulfur compounds while keeping the crunch intact. Drain and pat dry with paper towels.

8. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 6 equal portions (approximately 150g each). Gently form each into a patty about 4 inches in diameter and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb to prevent doming. Season both sides generously with kosher salt and black pepper immediately before cooking. Do not overwork the meat.

9. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet or griddle over high heat until smoking. Place patties in the pan without crowding. Cook undisturbed for 3 minutes on the first side to develop a deep sear.

10. Flip the patties and immediately lay 2 to 3 slices of Edam cheese over each. Cook for 2 to 2.5 minutes more. For medium rare, the internal temperature must read 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) on an instant-read thermometer. This is the only correct doneness.

11. Add a small splash of water to the skillet and immediately cover with a lid or dome for 30 seconds to create steam and melt the Edam completely over the patty. Remove patties to a rack and rest for 3 minutes.
12. Toast the buns: Butter the cut sides of each bun and place butter-side down on the still-hot skillet over medium heat. Toast until golden and crisp, about 1 minute.

13. Assemble: Spread the sauce on both cut sides of the bun. Layer green leaf lettuce on the bottom bun, followed by a tomato slice. Place the cheese-covered patty on top. Pile several drained raw onion rounds directly on top of the cheese. Cap with the top bun. Serve immediately.
